975.bp: Spotify needs to show ads and promote podcasts to listeners, but new advertisers or new podcast promotions often have barely any data about what works—so the system starts cold and has to guess. The challenge: how do you recommend something promising when you've never seen it before, without annoying users or wasting money on bad bets?
975.wh: The straightforward way—train separate models for ads and separate ones for promotions—means each new advertiser or campaign starts from scratch with no history. You'd need mountains of data before you could know if an ad actually converts. Meanwhile, shared knowledge across similar campaigns gets thrown away, and maintaining different models creates silos that are expensive and brittle.

Existing separate pipelines waste knowledge: when one advertiser learns what kinds of users stream indie folk, that insight dies there. New advertisers can't borrow it. The system also has to pick between optimizing just clicks or just streams, not both—but real business needs juggle multiple goals at once.
975.ap: The team built one unified model that learns from the entire history of ads and promotions together, using a shared foundation of user features, content, and context. When a new advertiser arrives, the model isn't starting blind—it draws on patterns learned from hundreds of past campaigns, then fine-tunes itself to that specific advertiser's data. The model simultaneously optimizes for multiple outcomes (streams, clicks, follows) like a multi-purpose engine.
975.ww: When you learn from many related tasks together, you pick up general principles: which kinds of users care about podcasts, how context shifts behavior, what creative elements attract attention. A new advertiser inherits these deep patterns instantly, then just adapts them slightly to their own niche. Optimizing multiple goals simultaneously actually helps—one goal's signal steers the model away from cheating the others.
975.po: In real testing on Spotify, the unified model cut the cost to get a listener to stream a podcast by 22%, and increased stream rates by 18–24%. The gains were sharpest for small, lesser-known podcasts that would normally starve for attention. The system also became simpler to run and scale—one model to maintain instead of dozens.

976.bp: Networks are everywhere—social ties reshape opinions, brains rewire themselves as they learn, power grids shift as demand changes. The real world rarely gives us perfect knowledge of these systems. Epidemiologists don't know every contact that could spread disease, power engineers don't know next year's demand exactly. How do you predict what a network will do when you can't fully describe it?
976.wh: A network's shape and weights determine everything: whether it spreads information fast or slow, whether it collapses under stress, whether it finds balance or spirals into chaos. But real-world networks hide from us—edges flicker, weights shift, nodes appear and vanish. If you ignore this incompleteness and pretend you have the true network, your predictions will be confidently wrong.

Standard dynamical network analysis assumes you know the network structure exactly. It ignores that contact patterns are uncertain, transmission rates fluctuate, or that the network itself changes over time. You can't just slot in guesses and hope—uncertainty itself changes how the system behaves.
976.ap: This tutorial brings together two usually separate fields: the science of networks in motion, and the art of tracking and quantifying uncertainty. It teaches techniques for asking not just 'what will happen?' but 'how wrong could I be, and how does that wrongness propagate through the network?'
976.ww: When you systematically track uncertainty, you spot which parts of the network matter most (maybe a few key hubs, or a fragile link). You can design robustness: if edge weight X is uncertain, what structure keeps the system stable anyway? You shift from false precision to honest prediction.
976.po: Practitioners learn practical methods for modeling epidemics, power grids, and neural adaptation with incomplete information, discovering which uncertainties sink predictions and which ones stay tolerable.

977.bp: Graph neural networks have proven powerful for tasks like social network recommendation, molecule classification, and fraud detection. But real-world graphs are gigantic—millions of nodes, billions of edges. Training models on graphs this large is slow and expensive. Can we compress a graph to one-tenth its size and still answer the same questions accurately?
977.wh: The naive way—just delete nodes or edges—destroys structure and information immediately. You need a compressed graph that still 'looks like' the original in ways that matter for prediction. Most existing work focuses only on copying node features, ignoring that the connections themselves are what give graphs their power. Dense representations waste space and can trap noise.

Existing graph compression methods copy features pixel-by-pixel but skip the relational skeleton. They also produce dense, redundant condensed graphs that don't save much memory or computation. The condensed graph becomes just another unhappy middle ground.
977.ap: The researchers designed a framework that represents many nodes by discrete codes (like having a alphabet of node types in the codebook), then uses low-rank matrix math to preserve the connection patterns from the original graph. Node features themselves get compressed losslessly by breaking them into compact discrete pieces.
977.ww: Discrete codes work like a vocabulary: instead of storing every node's float vector, you store which code it matches, massively shrinking memory. Low-rank approximation of graph connections means you capture the broad 'traffic patterns' of the network without storing every edge. Together, you get a graph that runs faster, uses less memory, but still sees the same structural patterns.
977.po: The compressed graph preserves accuracy on downstream tasks while slashing storage and computation time. It removes noise (redundancy in features) while locking in structure, making the condensed graph more efficient than the original for prediction.

978.bp: Graph neural networks now make decisions in high-stakes domains—fraud detection in financial networks, content moderation on social platforms, diagnostic systems for diseases. If someone can subtly poison the network (adding fake accounts, injecting false links), they can trick the model into wrong decisions. How do you attack these systems invisibly?
978.wh: Most attacks need a fake copy of the model to practice on, which often doesn't match the real one. Graph data is discrete (you add or remove an edge, not 0.6 of an edge), so finding adversarial changes is like searching through a huge space of broken combinations. Real defenses make attacks much harder, but existing attack methods weren't designed to handle them.

Surrogate models leak information but also misalign with reality. Discrete graph structures make gradient-based attacks fail. Most attack papers ignore defending systems, making them look stronger than they'd be in practice.
978.ap: The team built a reinforcement learning system that learns to inject nodes (fake accounts) and edges (false links) by trial and error, without needing a copy of the real model. It softens the discrete choices to avoid dead ends, designs a smarter edge sampler that respects graph topology, and explicitly learns what defenses expect so it can evade them.
978.ww: Learning by trial and error on the real system (feedback-only) is slower but honest—you're actually measuring against what you'll face. Softening discrete choices helps you escape local dead ends (you can't improve by 0.1 edge, but the algorithm treats it as if you could, then rounds at the end). Understanding defense mechanisms means you stop building attacks for 'ideal' systems and actually threaten real ones.
978.po: The attack method successfully fools graph neural networks even when those networks have built-in defenses, and it does so stealthily—the injected nodes and fake links look plausible, making the attack hard to detect.

979.bp: When you search a knowledge base—finding co-authors, tracking treatment paths, tracing idea lineage—the answer often lies in a multi-step journey: paper to author to paper, or symptom to drug to outcome. These paths follow patterns, but those patterns are hidden in the data and never written down. How do you find them automatically?
979.wh: Knowledge base designers write retrieval rules by hand: 'to find related papers, look through author lists.' But there are hundreds of possible retrieval patterns, and they differ by domain and task. You can't handcode them all. And when you do write them, they're rigid—maybe perfect for one task, useless for another.

Manual rules don't scale. Rules that work for one knowledge base fail on another. Rules that work today become stale as the domain evolves. You need the system to discover patterns by watching downstream tasks succeed or fail.
979.ap: The system learns retrieval rules by watching real feedback. When it gets a hint that a paper-to-paper query should succeed (maybe users clicked on a result), it explores: did the rule 'go through co-authors' work better than 'go through venues'? A reinforcement learning layer picks promising rules, then a second layer refines the scoring function for those rules, iterating together.
979.ww: By coupling rule discovery with retrieval refinement, the system doesn't waste time on rules that sound logical but don't work in practice. The feedback loop means rules adapt as the task changes. Jointly optimizing rules and scores means a mediocre rule with great scoring beats a perfect rule with bad scoring.
979.po: The system discovers retrieval patterns automatically and matches retrieval quality achieved by hand-coded rules—sometimes surpassing them—without requiring human domain expertise upfront.

980.bp: Recommendation systems use graphs of user-item interactions (a person clicks a movie, a user follows an artist) to predict what someone will like next. Learning from these patterns works well for popular items, but lesser-known items get barely clicked, so the system never learns good representations for them. How do you recommend the obscure stuff?
980.wh: Popular items flood with interaction signals; rare items starve. If an album has five plays, your representation of it is fragile—one more play flips its entire meaning. Most contrastive learning methods boost signals by randomly shuffling the graph, but random shuffling might destroy the structural skeleton that made the graph useful in the first place.
Random graph augmentation is crude. For long-tail items, random changes can wipe out the little signal there is. You need augmentation that preserves structure while adding diverse views.
980.ap: The researchers use a diffusion model (a process that adds noise, then carefully removes it) to create multiple views of the graph. First, they compress the graph to its structural essence using matrix math, which speeds up the diffusion. Then the diffusion model creates views that keep the graph structure but vary details. For rare items specifically, they guide the denoising by telling it: 'this should look like the broader graph,' using global structure as a helpful constraint.
980.ww: Diffusion processes can be precise about what to change and what to preserve—noise and signal separate cleanly. Compression captures the big-picture structure before creating views, so no view accidentally tosses the skeleton. For long-tail items, global constraints act as a lifeline: 'use what you learned from popular items to help predict this rare one.'
980.po: The system learns better representations for rare items by anchoring them to the overall graph structure, improving recommendation quality especially for the obscure content that platforms neglect.

981.bp: Recommendation systems at scale (YouTube, TikTok, Spotify) often generate textual identifiers for what to show next—not human-readable text, but a learned 'semantic ID' that compresses everything the system knows about a user or video into one token. The challenge: that ID needs to bring together different types of data (video features, creator info, transcripts) that speak different languages. How do you make one ID that understands them all?
981.wh: Images, graphs, and text each have their own structure and meaning. A creator's network relationships (who they collab with) don't look like what a vision model sees in the video thumbnail. An LLM trained on descriptions understands concepts differently than a graph model sees connections. Naively concatenating all these features creates a jumble where one modality drowns out others.
Different modalities compete. If you just concatenate features, text dominates, graph signals get lost. Different data types need alignment—translation into a shared meaning space.
981.ap: The team built a general framework (SEALNet) that aligns the semantics of each modality: it learns how to interpret the graph's signals in terms of the image's signals, how to translate the LLM's meaning into a common language. Once aligned, features merge into a single learned semantic ID. They demonstrate two flavors: one blends video understanding with creator collaboration networks, another weaves in LLM-based semantic understanding.
981.ww: Alignment lets you ask 'what does this collaboration graph statement mean in terms of video content?' and get a coherent answer. The shared semantic space is learned, not hand-coded, so it adapts to what actually matters for recommendation. Different modalities then contribute honestly to the same ID instead of fighting.
981.po: A single semantic ID now captures meaning across modalities, letting large-scale systems generate personalized recommendations using unified learned representations grounded in video, creator networks, and LLM understanding simultaneously.

982.bp: Fake news detectors are trained to spot false articles, but attackers can bypass them by adding comments (like 'I saw this firsthand' or 'peer-reviewed study confirms it') that shift a reader's belief in the article's truthfulness. How can attackers generate comments that fool the detector without human raters noticing the manipulation?
982.wh: Most attacks either modify the article text itself (obvious to readers) or grab generic comments from the web (and don't know which parts of a comment actually sway the detector's decision). Comment-based attacks are underexplored because it's not clear how to make comments that are both realistic and strategically damaging.

Generic comments don't exploit what the detector actually uses to decide. You need surgical precision: identify the tokens (words/phrases) that the detector leans on most, then craft comments that use those very tokens but twist their meaning.
982.ap: The attack system uses an explainability tool (SHAP) to identify which words the detector considers most important for real vs. fake judgments. Then it prompts an LLM: 'Write a human-like comment using these strategic words,' and the LLM generates realistic-looking text. Those comments get added to the article and tested against several published detectors (TextCNN, RoBERTa, dEFEND).
982.ww: Explainability reveals what the detector actually relies on (not what designers hoped it relies on). An LLM's job is to make natural text, so prompting it for comments that include strategic words yields human-sounding but adversarial comments. The combination respects what the detector 'sees' while evading what detectors 'expect' to see in natural comments.
982.po: The attack successfully fools state-of-the-art fake news detectors by appending LLM-generated comments, and the generated comments read naturally—they'd pass human readers' scrutiny because they use realistic language while weaponizing words the detector over-relies on.

983.bp: LLMs can now edit text fluently. An attacker could subtly reword news to shift how credible it seems—removing a qualifying phrase, tweaking a causal claim—without making it obviously false. How much can such small edits sway human belief? And how hard is it for an LLM to find the right edits?
983.wh: Most disinformation research focuses on fully synthetic fake articles or crude paraphrasing. But real propaganda is subtle—it doesn't announce itself. If you edit a claim from 'Police said they suspect the protester' to 'Police suspect the protester,' you've moved from reporting to accusation in seven characters. How would you even find such edits systematically?
Small edits hide from human scrutiny but can flip perception. Finding them requires understanding causal language, qualifying statements, and credibility markers. Brute-force search is impractical.
983.ap: The researchers had an LLM make targeted edits to news articles—removing hedging language ('said,' 'might'), shifting causal claims, introducing opposing evidence—while keeping the core story intact. They focused on four kinds of subtle, credibility-shifting changes that preserve readability. Then they measured: do human readers judge edited articles as more or less believable?
983.ww: Causal and hedging language are how writers signal certainty. An LLM trained on real text understands these nuances implicitly—it knows that removing 'reportedly' hardens a claim's perceived strength, or that adding counter-evidence seeds doubt. Small changes in these markers shift the article's tone from 'information' to 'accusation' or 'speculation.'
983.po: The work demonstrates that LLM-crafted minimal edits reliably shift human perception of news credibility—small, hard-to-spot changes move readers' judgment, proving that subtle adversarial manipulation of believability is both achievable and effective.

984.bp: Can a code generation model (ChatGPT, Codex, Claude) solve a competitive programming problem? Testing just the final code ('does it run?') misses half the story—you miss whether the model understood the problem, whether it picked the right algorithmic strategy, and whether it could explain its approach. How do you evaluate the actual thinking, not just the output?
984.wh: Standard benchmarks (LeetCode pass@k scores) measure 'did the code work?', ignoring that a model might get lucky or brute-force the solution. They don't tell you if the model grasped the problem structure or just memorized similar patterns. A model might fail the test but show brilliant reasoning partway through, or pass the test but for the wrong reasons.

Pass@k metrics are binary: code works or doesn't. This hides whether failures come from bad problem understanding, weak algorithm selection, or sloppy coding. It doesn't measure what matters for real programming: reasoning and problem-solving.
984.ap: The researchers built a four-phase evaluation benchmark: first, does the model understand the problem's examples? Second, does it select a sensible algorithm? Third, can it describe a solution approach? Fourth, does the code work? Each phase has intermediate checkpoints, graded by an LLM with specialized instructions. They curated 197 hand-picked competitive programming problems from Codeforces.
984.ww: Decomposing code generation into phases lets you see where the model breaks down. If it fails phase two (algorithm selection), that's a different weakness than failing phase four (coding). Each phase depends on the last—if a model doesn't understand the problem, no algorithm will save it. This dependency structure reveals whether code failures are surface-level or deep.
984.po: The benchmark reveals consistent gaps in code generation models' understanding and algorithmic reasoning, showing that models pass@k scores don't capture real weaknesses, and that each reasoning phase's quality directly predicts the next one's performance.

985.bp: Large language models can now act as judges in information retrieval—deciding if a document is relevant to a query. But they're susceptible to bias: if they just judged three documents as relevant, they're more likely to judge the fourth one relevant too, regardless of its actual content. Psychologists call this 'priming'—and it skews judgments silently. Can we teach an LLM to resist this?
985.wh: Priming happens because humans are susceptible to context: after seeing 'good examples,' your threshold for what counts as 'good' shifts. LLMs likely do the same—the model's output at step N depends on its outputs at steps 1 through N-1. Randomizing order helps, but doesn't solve it. And we don't have a reliable technique to suppress it in LLMs specifically.
Simple fixes like randomizing order or flushing memory work partially but not fully. The problem runs deep in how models process context.
985.ap: The team tested whether simulated personalities reduce priming. In psychology, personality traits (like openness or neuroticism) correlate with bias susceptibility. They prompted LLMs to adopt Big Five personality profiles (which psychologically correspond to various trait levels), then measured priming on relevance labeling tasks from TREC 2021 and 2022.
985.ww: Personality frameworks are psychologically grounded—they've been shown to predict bias in humans. When an LLM adopts a 'high openness, low neuroticism' profile, it may adopt the cognitive patterns those traits typically exhibit, including resistance to priming. Simulating personalities essentially borrows psychological knowledge about robust human judgment.
985.po: Certain personality profiles (notably high openness, low neuroticism) consistently reduce the LLM's susceptibility to priming, and this holds across multiple LLM models and task types, suggesting personality prompting as a practical technique to improve LLM-based relevance judging.

986.bp: YouTube recommends billions of videos daily, shaping what people watch and believe. Is the algorithm trapping users in filter bubbles, serving them only content that mirrors their existing views? Auditing this at scale is nearly impossible—you can't fake being millions of different users without getting caught. How can researchers reproducibly and ethically test what YouTube actually recommends?
986.wh: Real user testing is slow, unethical, and violates terms of service. Simulating many diverse users automatically requires mimicking realistic behavior (not robotic sequences), tracking what each persona sees over time, handling the messy complexity of how recommendations change moment-to-moment, and doing it all reproducibly so other researchers can verify the findings.

Scale, realism, reproducibility, and ethics all pull in different directions. A simple bot gets caught. A large-scale audit with real accounts is unethical and violates terms. Existing tools don't let you compare different personas' recommendation paths transparently.
986.ap: TRACE is an open framework that automates browsers like humans would, creating simulated personas with specific interests and demographic profiles (via LLM-based persona generation). It runs experiments on YouTube at scale, logs everything to a database for traceability, and uses LLMs to synthesize context-aware behaviors so personas act realistically rather than robotically.
986.ww: Containerized browser automation is practical and difficult to detect. LLM-driven personas generate natural sequences of searches and clicks—not hardcoded patterns—making the simulation realistic. Database-backed logging means every decision is recorded, so other researchers can audit your methodology and reproduce your findings. The modular design lets researchers swap in different personas or behavioral strategies.
986.po: TRACE enables large-scale, reproducible, transparent audits of YouTube's recommendation ecosystem, allowing researchers to empirically test whether personalization creates filter bubbles and to share findings in a verifiable, ethically grounded way.

987.bp: You have some money to invest. You're willing to take risk, but you want good returns. How much should you put in tech stocks vs. bonds vs. emerging markets? This is portfolio optimization—balancing diverse assets under your risk tolerance. Most optimization methods find one best answer. But different investors have different appetites for risk. How do you flexibly generate many good portfolios across risk levels?
987.wh: Deterministic models (gradient descent on a fixed objective) find one optimal portfolio, then you're stuck with it. Changing your risk tolerance means retraining. Stochastic methods that randomly sample portfolios usually require multi-stage training pipelines that are complicated and don't directly optimize for portfolio quality. You're optimizing a proxy (next-day prices) instead of the real goal (good portfolio allocation).
Flexible methods are complex. Direct methods are rigid. Neither handles risk preference smoothly.
987.ap: The researchers use a diffusion model—a process that starts with random noise and iteratively refines it into clean structure—to generate portfolios directly. The diffusion process has a built-in 'risk guidance' mechanism: you can adjust a dial that biases the refinement toward either high-risk or low-risk outcomes without retraining. The model learns the distribution of good portfolios from historical market data.
987.ww: Diffusion models are built to gradually transform noise into fine structure, and that process is reversible—you can steer it mid-way using guidance signals. Risk guidance means the same trained model adapts to any risk level instantly, like turning a knob. The model learns to sample from the distribution of actually good portfolios, not to forecast future prices (which is hard) or optimize a surrogate objective (which can diverge from the true goal).
987.po: The diffusion model generates diverse, high-quality portfolios at any risk level, outperforming baselines in returns, risk management, and overall reliability across real market datasets.

988.bp: Recommender systems decide what movies, music, and products get promoted to you. A malicious actor could inject fake user accounts that rate things artificially high or low, shifting the system's recommendations to favor certain items or creators. These 'shilling attacks' threaten system integrity. How can someone attack a recommender using LLM-generated fake users and reviews?
988.wh: Existing shilling attacks use simplistic rules to generate fake interactions—they might rate an item '5 stars' repeatedly, but that pattern is obviously fake. Real defenses look for these obvious patterns. Also, most attacks ignore user reviews (just ratings), which limits how realistic the fake user looks. Existing methods need access to the system's internals to work well.

Simple attacks are detectable. Ignoring reviews means the fake users are incomplete. Low-knowledge attacks (using only what an attacker can observe from outside) usually don't work well against defended systems.
988.ap: The team built AgentSA, a framework that uses LLM-based agents to generate fake user profiles. The agents read target items, generate plausible reviews (using an LLM), select what to rate (guided by targeted mechanisms that maximize impact), and maintain a memory of what they've 'done' to stay consistent. All of this is coordinated to maximize manipulation while avoiding detection.
988.ww: LLMs are trained on real human text, so reviews they generate sound natural. Multiple agents coordinating means attack patterns aren't just one user doing obvious things—it looks like varied, independent behavior. Targeting mechanisms ensure fake interactions push the system in intended directions. Behavioral camouflage (staying consistent, not doing anything too obviously weird) makes the attack stealthy.
988.po: LLM agents can execute shilling attacks that consistently outperform existing methods in both effectiveness (manipulating recommendations) and stealth (avoiding detection), revealing a new class of threats to recommender systems enabled by sophisticated LLM-based impersonation.

989.bp: When an LLM recommends something, can it explain why? 'Because your taste resembles other users who liked it' is one kind of reason. But LLMs have their own knowledge base—they know that sci-fi fans often enjoy certain themes. Recommendations work better when the system uses both collaborative patterns (what similar users did) and LLM knowledge (semantic meaning). The hard part: explaining how those two sources align. Can an LLM generate coherent rationales bridging both?
989.wh: LLMs understand concepts in natural language. Collaborative recommenders work on user-item interaction patterns. These live in different universes: 'users similar to you liked this' doesn't sound like 'this book explores the same themes you enjoy.' There's a semantic gap. A system might make a great recommendation but fail to explain it because the reasoning doesn't bridge the gap, leaving users confused about why they got that suggestion.
The semantic gap blocks explainability. LLM knowledge and collaborative signals speak different languages. Direct fusion doesn't produce coherent explanations.
989.ap: ARROW (Adaptive Reasoning for LLM-based Recommendation With explainability) uses chain-of-thought prompting—asking the LLM to 'think out loud' about why a recommendation fits. It then measures the uncertainty of that reasoning using statistical tests, and adaptively adjusts how much weight to give the reasoning vs. the collaborative signal. When the reasoning is confident and coherent, it dominates the decision; when uncertain, collaborative signals take over.
989.ww: Chain-of-thought reasoning lets an LLM articulate semantic connections between user preferences and item meaning. Uncertainty quantification prevents the model from confidently BS-ing—if the reasoning is shaky, the system knows to distrust it. Adaptive weighting means you get human-interpretable explanations when possible, but fall back to reliable collaborative signals when reasoning breaks down.
989.po: ARROW produces recommendations with human-interpretable explanations by bridging LLM semantic understanding and collaborative patterns, achieving strong accuracy while providing coherent rationales for why each item was recommended.
